title: Mastering Negative and Interrogative Structures in Healthtech
body:
In English, we use the auxiliary verbs 'do' and 'does' to form negatives and questions in the present simple. For negatives, we add 'not' to the auxiliary: 'do not' (don't) or 'does not' (doesn't). Remember that 'doesn't' is used only for third-person singular (he, she, it, or a singular noun like 'the product' or 'the patient'). When we use 'does/doesn't', the main verb loses its '-s' ending because the auxiliary already carries the marker. For questions, we place 'Do' or 'Does' at the beginning of the sentence. For open questions (WH- questions), we place the question word (What, Where, Why, How) before the auxiliary.

In a startup environment, you use these daily to manage expectations. You might say, 'The CEO doesn't approve the new UI design yet' or 'Do we meet the HIPAA compliance standards?'. A common mistake for Spanish speakers is to ignore the auxiliary and add 'not' directly to the main verb (e.g., 'The product not work' instead of 'The product doesn't work'). Another frequent error is using 'does' with a verb ending in 's' (e.g., 'Does he likes the demo?' instead of 'Does he like the demo?'). Always keep the auxiliary as the 'carrier' of the tense.
keyPoints: Use 'don't' for I, you, we, they; use 'doesn't' for he, she, it.
Remove the '-s' from the main verb when using 'doesn't'.
Place 'Do/Does' before the subject for yes/no questions.
WH- words (What, How) come before the auxiliary verb.
Never use 'not' directly with main verbs like 'like' or 'work'.

title: Memo: Troubleshooting the Patient Portal
body:
To: Engineering Team
From: Product Lead

Hi team, we need to address the performance issues in our patient-facing portal. We know the current build doesn't sync with the electronic health records (EHR) correctly. Does the backend team have the latest API documentation? We don't see the integration logs on the dashboard. Also, why does the interface crash during the login process? The investors expect a stable release by Friday. 

We don't need a full overhaul today, but we must fix the connection bug. Does the system recognize the user authentication tokens? If it doesn't, the security audit will fail. Please check if the database query is too slow. What does the terminal report when you run the test script? Let's fix this before the demo for the Series A investors. We don't want to show a broken product.
keyPoints: Does the system recognize tokens?
We don't see the logs.
Why does the interface crash?
The team doesn't have a stable build yet.
Investors don't want to see a broken demo.

title: Drafting a Product Inquiry
body: Write a 150-word email to your CTO asking about the status of a new healthtech feature (e.g., telemedicine video integration or automated prescription refills). You must include at least two negative sentences using 'don't' or 'doesn't' and two questions using 'Do' or 'Does'. Use the context of preparing for a meeting with a hospital board of directors or a potential partner. Ensure you are professional and concise as required by Silicon Valley communication standards.
keyPoints: Use at least two negative sentences (don't/doesn't).
Use at least two questions (Do/Does).
Maintain a professional, startup-focused tone.
Address a specific technical feature.
Explain the impact of the feature on the product timeline.

title: The Interface Audit
body: Sofia stares at the screen. The latency issue is solved, but the current UI prototype feels clunky. Dr. Aris, their lead clinical consultant, is arriving in two hours to review the surgery tracking module. Sofia turns to Mateo, who is still tweaking the CSS. 'He doesn’t understand why the icons are so small,' Sofia says, pointing to the feedback logs. Mateo sighs, rubbing his eyes. 'I don’t agree,' he replies, 'but I see his point.' They need a clean, intuitive layout, yet they don’t have time for a total rewrite. Sofia looks at the task list. 'Does the system prioritize urgent patient data?' she asks, tapping a button that does nothing. Mateo shakes his head. 'It doesn’t prioritize anything yet because we haven’t mapped the workflow.' The pressure mounts. They have ninety minutes to simplify the dashboard for a surgeon who doesn’t care about backend architecture; he only cares about real-time metrics during a high-stakes procedure. Sofia makes a decision: they will strip away the secondary charts to reduce cognitive load. 'Does this layout work better for a surgeon in a sterile environment?' she asks. Mateo nods, finally seeing the vision. He removes the unnecessary panels, and suddenly, the path to the patient vitals is clear. The interface now flows with purpose. When Dr. Aris arrives, he interacts with the system without hesitation. He doesn’t ask for further modifications; he simply starts testing the emergency alert trigger. The feedback is immediate and positive. They have successfully bridged the gap between complex data and clinical necessity, ensuring that the surgeon can trust the software when seconds matter most. As the session concludes, Sofia notes that while the logic holds, the team must address how the platform handles individual user preferences over long, shifting rotations.
keyPoints: Use 'Does' for singular subjects (the platform, your team).
Use 'Do' for plural subjects (competitors, investors).
Keep short answers simple: 'Yes, it does' or 'No, they don't'.
Use Wh- words for open questions: 'What does your team need?'
Avoid adding 's' to the verb after 'does' (e.g., 'Does it works?' is incorrect).
